rationale: The entry's core identification — a garden as a planted stand of trees where the trees are nations/peoples and God is the gardener who rules them — is carried directly by the single text printed with the entry. Ezekiel 31 is one of the few passages in Scripture that decodes its own imagery: Assyria is 'a cedar in Lebanon' (31:3), the LORD says 'I have made him fair by the multitude of his branches: so that all the trees of Eden, that were in the garden of God, envied him' (31:9), and the chapter closes by naming the referent outright — 'This is Pharaoh and all his multitude' (31:18). Within that chapter the 'trees of Eden' envy a rival, are 'comforted in the nether parts of the earth,' and 'went down into hell with him unto them that be slain with the sword' (31:16-17) — behavior impossible for literal paradise flora and natural for fallen kings and their peoples. The garden of God in this passage is therefore a field of nation-trees under God's cultivating rule, exactly as the entry states. The strongest counter — the mainstream 'garden = paradise/divine presence' reading — is a true account of Genesis 2-3 and Revelation 21-22 as narrative settings, but as a rival symbolic identification of the cited text it cannot explain why Eden's trees envy Assyria, descend to Sheol, and are named as Pharaoh and his multitude. The chapter's supporting pattern (Daniel 4's tree decoded as the king, Ezekiel 17's 'all the trees of the field' as the powers God fells and exalts, Hosea's vine, Jeremiah's olive) shows the tree-as-nation equation is repeatedly self-decoded by Scripture, which grounds the 'gardener's rule' clause via Ezekiel 17:24 and Daniel 4. Every assertion actually printed in the entry — planted grouping of trees, trees as nations/peoples, arrangement under a gardener's rule — is supported by the cited text and cross-texts, so support is FULL. Objections to the chapter's further applications (Isaiah 1/65/66 gardens as nations, the eternal-diet argument) are out of scope and preserved separately.
book_core_identification: In the Bible's symbolic register, a 'garden' is a planted grouping of trees where the trees are nations or peoples, set together under God's rule as the gardener — with the garden of God in Ezekiel 31 as the paradigm case (trees of Eden = Pharaoh, Assyria, and their multitudes).
book_secondary_elaborations: The trees composing the garden are specifically nations or peoples (not merely individuals).
The nations are 'arranged together' as a planted, ordered stand rather than a wild forest.
The garden stands under a gardener's rule — God as the one who plants, beautifies, fells, and exalts the trees (Ezek 31:9 'I have made him fair'; Ezek 17:24).
chapter_only_objections: The rereading of Isaiah 1:29-30 and 65:3 ('gardens' as the nations Judah ran to rather than literal pagan cult-groves) is a chapter application not asserted in the entry; the literal grove-cult reading remains the majority scholarly view of those passages.
The Isaiah 66:17 argument ('behind one tree in the midst' with 'tree' supplied by translators, read as following one nation) is a chapter-level textual claim not printed in the entry.
The inference that the clean/unclean food law is eternally binding because Isaiah 66:17's judgment mentions swine's flesh is a doctrinal extension found only in the chapter.
The broader system-claims (sea = unrooted peoples, beasts = ravening nations, mountain = kingdom, grass = mortal flesh) are separate glossary entries/chapter claims, not assertions of this entry.
The reading of Peter's Acts 10 vision ('kill and eat' as covenant-making language) is chapter-only.
strongest_counter_interpretation: The garden is Scripture's master image of paradise — Eden as the place of God's presence, life, and unbroken fellowship with humanity, lost at the fall and restored in the new creation (Genesis 2-3; Isaiah 51:3; Revelation 22:1-5). On this reading, Ezekiel 31's 'trees of Eden in the garden of God' are the legendary magnificent trees of the paradise garden, invoked merely as a poetic standard of beauty and grandeur that Assyria surpassed — not themselves symbolic nations.
counter_core_identification: Garden = paradise, the place of divine presence and blessedness; the trees of Eden in Ezekiel 31:9 are literal/mythic paradise trees used as a comparative standard of splendor, not coded nations.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that the garden's constituent trees are nations or peoples: it holds that the garden signifies a place (paradise/divine presence) rather than a corporate arrangement of nation-trees, so the two identifications cannot both be the symbolic referent of the garden in the cited text.
counter_case: The overwhelming canonical usage of 'garden' (Genesis 2-3; Isaiah 51:3; Ezekiel 36:35; Revelation 22) concerns paradise and God's dwelling, not groupings of nations.

Ezekiel 31 could be read as a hyperbolic comparison: Assyria was so magnificent that even Eden's fabled trees envied it — the trees function as a benchmark of beauty, not as decoded political entities.

Ezekiel 28:13 places the king of Tyre 'in Eden the garden of God' in a similarly allusive, mythic-poetic register, suggesting Eden imagery in Ezekiel is evocative background rather than a fixed symbol-system.

All four blinded common-interpretation responses converge on paradise/divine presence as the primary meaning, with no alternative listing 'grouping of nations' at all — indicating the book's definition is idiosyncratic relative to the interpretive tradition.
book_explanatory_advantages: Ezekiel 31 self-decodes: 'This is Pharaoh and all his multitude' (31:18) explicitly names the tree as a nation with its people, and Assyria is the cedar (31:3), so the trees standing in the garden of God in this very chapter are demonstrably nations.

The trees of Eden 'went down into hell with him unto them that be slain with the sword' and are 'comforted in the nether parts of the earth' (31:16-17) — coherent if they are fallen kings/nations in Sheol, incoherent if they are literal paradise trees.

Trees envying (31:9) is personal, political behavior; the book's reading requires no personification patch, while the counter must treat envy, descent to Sheol, and comfort among the slain all as extended poetic decoration.

The 'gardener's rule' clause matches God's stated activity: 'I have made him fair' (31:9), 'I the LORD have brought down the high tree, have exalted the low tree' before 'all the trees of the field' (Ezek 17:24), and Daniel 4's decree to hew down the king-tree — God cultivating and felling nation-trees.

The tree = king/nation equation is independently established by Scripture's own explicit keys (Daniel 4:20-22 'It is thou, O king'; Ezekiel 17:12; Hosea 10:1; Jeremiah 11:16), satisfying the book's multiple-witness standard, so a garden of such trees being a grouping of nations is a small, disciplined step.
counter_explanatory_advantages: It matches the dominant canonical and traditional usage of 'garden' across Genesis, the prophets' restoration oracles, and Revelation.
It requires no symbolic system at all for Genesis 2-3 read as narrative setting.
It preserves the widely held Eden-to-New-Jerusalem arc that all four blinded responses identify.
decisive_sources: Ezekiel 31:3, 9, 16-18 — the cedar is Assyria, the envying trees of Eden descend to Sheol with the slain, and the chapter's own key names the tree: 'This is Pharaoh and all his multitude.'
Daniel 4:20-22 — Scripture's explicit decoding of a great tree as the king and his dominion, establishing the tree-nation equation the garden definition builds on.
Ezekiel 17:22-24 — God as gardener among 'all the trees of the field,' bringing down the high tree and exalting the low, supporting the 'gardener's rule' clause.
unresolved_objections: The entry defines 'garden' generally, but the common paradise sense remains the natural reading of Genesis 2-3 as narrative; the entry is best defended as the symbolic-register meaning operative in prophetic texts like Ezekiel 31, and the glossary does not print that scoping qualification.
The counter-reading of Ezekiel 31:9 as pure hyperbole (Eden's trees as a beauty benchmark) is not absurd for verse 9 in isolation, though it fails at verses 16-18.
